channel.title: MIA — Management Intelligence Alert
channel.description: daily selected and enriched macroeconomic and political news

item.title: Chinatimes reports that UK consumer price inflation rose to 3.5% in September from 3.1% in August, with diesel and gasoline costs a key factor, and the Frankfurter Allgemeine says analysts now see a Bank of England rate rise as inevitable.
item.description:
Chinatimes, citing the Office for National Statistics, reports that the UK consumer price index rose by 3.5% year on year in September 2026, up from 3.1% in August, and that the ONS cited higher diesel and gasoline costs as a key factor. It says services price inflation reached 3.7%, up from 3.4% in August and above economists' estimate of 3.6%, and that core inflation, which excludes food, energy, alcohol and tobacco, rose from 2.6% to 2.8%. The Frankfurter Allgemeine, which gives the 3.5% as the August figure where Chinatimes gives September, says the rate was slightly higher than expected and that analysts and investors now consider an imminent rise in the key interest rate from 3.75% to 4.0% to be inevitable, with the next Bank of England meeting at the beginning of November. It cites the Deutsche Bank chief economist in London, Sanjay Raja, as expecting inflation to reach 4% by the turn of the year and likely to rise above that in winter, and the Bank of England to raise rates twice in the next few months. The rows do not give the date of the rate decision, the forecast for the September figure, or the contribution of each component.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows describe consumer prices and expectations of a rate rise, not a change in activity. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, inflation driven by fuel costs raises operating costs for manufacturers and transport, and a rate rise would raise financing costs for housing and investment. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, UK construction and manufacturing are customer groups, so higher financing costs could slow housing and project activity, and higher fuel costs could raise delivered costs of inputs, with the effect depending on how long inflation stays high. The rows give no figures for construction or for chemicals. Points that may be worth considering include the Bank of England's decision in early November, the next inflation release, and fuel and energy prices.

Chinatimes | Frankfurter Allgemeine

item.title: France's 10-year yield rose above 5% for the first time since 2002, La Vanguardia reports, with the spread over German bonds at 157 basis points there and 159.4 in Commercial Times, which dates it 21 October and says the yield briefly broke above 5%.
item.description:
La Vanguardia reports that on Wednesday the rate at which France finances itself for ten years passed 5% for the first time since 2002, with the difference from the German rate at 157 basis points, after a Tuesday close at 153 basis points that was the highest since November 2011. It says France now finances itself at a notably higher rate than Italy, at 4.57%, and Spain, at 4.06%, and that the 2027 draft budget foresees new efforts of EUR 43 billion to reduce the public deficit to 5% of GDP in 2027, although a compromise looks difficult in a deeply divided parliament a few months before the presidential election. Commercial Times says the benchmark yield briefly broke above 5%, a new high since 2002, and that the spread over German yields widened by 6 basis points to 159.4, a 15-year high, which it says has raised market concerns about a "Eurozone Debt Crisis 2.0". MarketScreener adds that the euro was down almost 1% in the month at USD 1.122, with France facing widespread anti-government protests and a worsening fiscal outlook. The rows do not give the closing yield, the level of German yields, or the date of a budget vote, and the two rows differ by about two basis points on the spread.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows describe market prices for French government debt, not a change in demand. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, higher government borrowing costs raise the cost of public financing and can pass into mortgage and corporate lending rates, which weighs on construction and investment decisions. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, French construction and manufacturing are customer groups, so higher financing costs could slow building projects and investment, while a wider spread within the euro area could raise financing costs more broadly. The rows give no figure for lending rates or for construction. Points that may be worth considering include the outcome of the budget debate, whether the spread widens beyond the 157 to 159.4 basis points reported, and the next central bank communications.

La Vanguardia | Commercial Times | MarketScreener

item.title: Anadolu reports China defended its rare-earth export curbs on Japan, answering a Financial Times report that Japan sought US help to ease them; Anadolu says the FT also reported Japan could exhaust its yttrium stocks within months.
item.description:
Anadolu reports that on 21 October Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Mao Ning defended China's rare-earth export restrictions on Japan, saying the measures were intended to prevent Japan's "remilitarization" and its efforts to acquire nuclear weapons. She was responding, the row says, to a Financial Times report that Japan had sought US assistance in persuading Beijing to ease the export controls amid dwindling supplies of yttrium, a critical rare-earth element. According to the row, the Financial Times reported that Japan could exhaust its yttrium stockpiles within months, potentially disrupting automotive, aerospace and semiconductor production. The row does not say when the restrictions were introduced, which products they cover or whether they are licence-based, how large Japan's stockpiles are, whether other rare earths are affected, or how Washington has responded. The statement on stockpiles is the Financial Times's as relayed by Anadolu; the row does not quote it.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The row combines an official Chinese statement with a newspaper report of a possible shortage. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a shortage of one critical material in a large manufacturing economy can slow production in the industries that use it, and export controls by a main supplier can affect other buyers over time. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, automotive, aerospace and electronics manufacturers are customer groups, so a production disruption in Japan could lower demand from those plants, while supply controls on critical materials could also affect other trading partners of China. The row gives no figure for output or for adhesives. Points that may be worth considering include the size of Japan's stocks, whether other countries face similar restrictions, and any agreement between the US and China on the matter.

Anadolu Agency

item.title: Canada and Ontario announce a support plan for steel and autos, put at CAD 9 billion by the Financial Post and lower by other outlets, with a CAD 5 billion steel fund, CAD 2.5 billion for autos and 2026 emission standards held to 2029.
item.description:
The Financial Post reports that Prime Minister Mark Carney announced on 21 October a CAD 9 billion partnership with Ontario to support the province's tariff-battered steel and auto industries. It says the steel package includes a joint CAD 5 billion fund over five years, with about a third from the Ontario government, that the federal and Ontario governments will provide a further CAD 2.5 billion over two years for large automotive capital projects, and that the government will hold off on raising federal vehicle emission standards, keeping them at 2026 levels through 2029. BNN Bloomberg gives the CAD 9 billion total and adds CAD 1 billion for the Ring of Fire mining development in northern Ontario. Other outlets give different totals: the Mainichi says CAD 8.7 billion, which it gives as USD 6.2 billion, MarketScreener says CAD 7.5 billion for automakers and steel plus CAD 1 billion for roads to mineral deposits, and Euronews says CAD 6.2 billion, equal to the Mainichi's USD 6.2 billion, so the currency of one of the two figures is unclear, with CAD 3.7 billion for steel and CAD 1.8 billion for autos over five years. Euronews also says Canadian auto exports to the US have fallen by more than 10% and US exports to Canada by more than 20%, and that Carney has set a target of doubling exports to non-US markets within a decade. The Mainichi row says Carney acknowledged that an integrated North American auto industry may no longer be a priority for Washington and that Trump has said he wants automakers to move production from Canada to the US, and CBC says Trump threatened in August to raise tariffs on cars, trucks, auto parts and steel to 50% on 1 January 2027. The components the rows name, CAD 5 billion, CAD 2.5 billion and CAD 1 billion, add to CAD 8.5 billion, below the CAD 9 billion total. The rows do not say which plants or projects will be funded, how much is grants rather than loans, the tariff rates now in force, or the period of the trade figures.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows describe a government support plan, not a change in tariffs or demand. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, support for capital projects and a pause in emission standards can help keep plants running and can shape which vehicles are built, while tariffs that split an integrated cross-border industry can move production and supplier choices. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, vehicle assembly and steel-using manufacturing are customer groups, so funding for auto capital projects could support investment in assembly and electric-vehicle capacity in Ontario, while weaker cross-border vehicle flows could lower volumes in the meantime. The rows give no figures for materials or for chemicals. Points that may be worth considering include the projects named when funds are allocated, the 1 January 2027 tariff threat, and the outcome of the Canada–EU summit.

Financial Post | BNN Bloomberg | MarketScreener | Mainichi | Euronews | CBC

item.title: Domain data show Australian capital-city house prices fell 4.7% in the September quarter, the largest quarterly fall on record, with declines in all eight state and territory capitals for the first time in 15 years.
item.description:
The Australian Broadcasting Corporation reports, citing Domain, that house prices in Australia declined by 4.7%, the steepest quarterly drop on record. Prices dropped in every capital city in the September quarter, the first time in 15 years and only the second time on record. The sharpest fall was in Perth, at 7.4%, and combined capital-city house prices fell to AUD 1,226,566. Sydney and Melbourne recorded their largest quarterly falls in four years, at 4.7% and 3.3%. Unit prices fell 3.5%, the second consecutive quarter in which both property types declined. Xinhua reports the same Domain report and says the downturn was attributed to lower buyer confidence because of cost-of-living pressures, interest rate rises and the federal government's move to wind back tax concessions for property investors. The rows do not give annual changes, sales volumes, building approvals or new-home sales, the size of the interest rate rises or of the tax change, or a split between new and existing homes.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows give median house prices, which does not measure construction activity. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a fall in house prices of this size can lower developers' margins and buyers' confidence, and building volumes follow with a lag. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, new housing and renovation use adhesive technologies in flooring, insulation and facades, so weaker housing demand could lower volumes from Australian residential building, although prices are a weaker guide to volumes than approvals or starts. The rows give no figures for building activity. Points that may be worth considering include building approvals and housing-finance data, whether prices keep falling in the December quarter, and the next interest rate decisions.

ABC | Xinhua

item.title: Handelsblatt reports a DIW Berlin study finds German construction labour productivity nearly 30% below its 2010 level in 2025, and warns that without a significant productivity gain, government investment threatens higher prices.
item.description:
Handelsblatt reports on a study by the German Institute for Economic Research (DIW Berlin), commissioned by the Bertelsmann Stiftung, which finds that without a significant increase in productivity in the German construction industry, government investment in the sector threatens to result in higher prices. According to the row, labour productivity in construction was nearly 30% below the 2010 level in 2025. The row says the negative trend appears in all construction sectors and company sizes, and that it accelerated after the Corona pandemic and with the interest rate and cost shock, especially since the war in Ukraine. The row does not say how productivity is measured, which government investment programmes the study refers to, how large a price rise it expects, or what the study recommends. It gives no figures for construction output, orders or prices.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The row describes a study of productivity and its link to prices, not a measure of building activity. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, if productivity does not rise, additional public spending could be absorbed by higher prices rather than by more building, so the volume of work and of materials that a given budget produces could be smaller than the budget suggests. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, construction is a customer group and adhesive technologies are used in facades, insulation and flooring, so volume growth from public investment in Germany could be smaller than headline budgets imply. The row gives no figure for materials. Points that may be worth considering include German construction output and orders, the size and timing of public infrastructure spending, and building-price indices.

Handelsblatt

item.title: The Economic Times reports Indian paint companies raised prices 10–15% since April and are expected to post 10–15% higher September-quarter revenue and profit, while analysts expect margins at many companies to fall 70–120 basis points.
item.description:
The Economic Times reports that domestic paint companies in India are expected to post 10–15% year-on-year growth in both revenue and profit for the September quarter, which it attributes to a series of price increases over the last few months. Since April, it says, companies have raised prices by 10–15%, with the market leader Asian Paints among those making the steepest increases. The row says the price rises help offset part of the increase in costs that the companies have seen in the last few months, but that analysts expect EBITDA (earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation) margins to fall for many companies by 70–120 basis points against the previous year. It expects Asian Paints to see a margin fall of more than 100 basis points and Kansai Nerolac Paints a fall of about 50 basis points, while Berger Paints India could see its margin improve because of a low base in the previous year. The row does not say which costs have risen, how much of the expected growth comes from volume rather than price, whether the 10–15% refers to list prices or realised prices, or what the companies' reported results are, since the results are expectations at the time of the row.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The row gives analysts' expectations for results that had not been published when it appeared. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, price rises of 10–15% that still leave margins lower would suggest that costs have risen by more than the companies have been able to pass on. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, paints and adhesive technologies draw on some of the same raw-material groups, such as resins and solvents, so cost pressure of this kind in coatings could also reach input costs and price discussions for adhesive producers in India, with the effect depending on contracts and on how much customers accept. The row names no raw material and gives no figure for adhesives. Points that may be worth considering include which input costs lie behind the margin pressure, the September-quarter results when they are published, and whether further price rises follow.

Economic Times

item.title: The Bundesbank no longer expects German GDP growth in the third quarter and expects significant growth in the fourth, depending on the Middle East war; harmonised inflation was 3.3% in September.
item.description:
Süddeutsche Zeitung and Handelsblatt report that the Bundesbank expects the German economy to grow significantly in the fourth quarter of 2026, with further recovery depending on the war in the Middle East. For the third quarter its economists no longer expect even minimal growth in gross domestic product, so the recovery has been temporarily interrupted after a positive first half. The rows attribute this to temporary burdens, above all low Rhine water levels that strain industrial supply chains, to a noticeable weakening of foreign trade at the start of the second half and to private consumption held back by high inflation. Anadolu, reporting the same Bundesbank assessment, says the economy likely stagnated, that inflation in September reached its highest level since late 2023 and that harmonised inflation rose to 3.3% from 2.9% in August as the Middle East conflict raised energy prices. It says that weakness in the automotive sector weighed on industrial production in August, that low water levels disrupted shipping and raised transport costs for energy-intensive industries, including oil refining and chemicals, that construction output rose in August although rising mortgage rates are expected to limit activity, and that the bank expects inflation to stay elevated as energy costs reach industrial goods, food and services. The rows do not give growth rates for either quarter, the size of the August output changes, or any figure for chemical output.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows report the Bundesbank's assessment, not published GDP data. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a flat third quarter with weaker foreign trade and high inflation points to softer demand from German industry and households, and higher inland-shipping costs add to the cost of moving raw materials to and from plants along the Rhine. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, German manufacturing and construction are customer groups, so weak automotive output and mortgage rates that are expected to limit building could hold back volumes in the near term, and higher transport costs could add to the delivered cost of chemical inputs, while the expected fourth-quarter growth depends on the course of the Middle East war. The rows give no figure for chemical or construction demand. Points that may be worth considering include the first official estimate of third-quarter GDP, Rhine water levels, and construction output and mortgage rates.

Süddeutsche Zeitung | Handelsblatt | Anadolu Agency

item.title: ANFAC data show Spain's vehicle production fell 1.6% year on year to 1.67 million units in the first nine months of 2026, while electrified vehicle output rose 13.1% to 195,335 units and electric car output rose 64%.
item.description:
La Gaceta reports that, according to the Spanish association of vehicle and truck manufacturers ANFAC, vehicle production in Spain fell 1.6% year on year to 1.67 million units in the first nine months of 2026, while production of electrified vehicles rose 13.1% to 195,335 units. El Correo, citing ANFAC, says that electrified vehicles, including pure electric and plug-in hybrids, were 11.7% of total production in the nine months and 18.2% in September, up 5.9 percentage points on September 2025. It says battery-electric vehicle output in September was 32,151 units, up 153.3% and 14.5% of the month's total volume, while plug-in hybrid output fell 43.3% in the month to 8,396 units. La Vanguardia, citing ANFAC data, says electric car production rose 64% in the nine months to nearly 102,000 units, with September's 29,653 units up 212%, and that new models at Martorell and in Navarra, among them the Cupra Raval, the Volkswagen ID.Polo, the Skoda Epiq and the ID.Cross, are driving the increase. The rows use different bases, electric cars, battery-electric vehicles including commercial vehicles, and electrified vehicles, so the September shares differ. They do not give production of combustion-engine vehicles, exports, a breakdown by plant, or the reason for the 1.6% fall.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows give ANFAC production counts, which measure output in Spain, not demand for vehicles. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a small fall in total output together with a shift towards electric models changes the mix of vehicles built, and new models can change the components and processes used. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, vehicle assembly and electric-vehicle batteries use adhesive technologies, so lower total output could lower volumes while the move to electric models could change which products are qualified at Spanish plants. The rows give no figures for materials. Points that may be worth considering include ANFAC's next monthly release, vehicle exports, and the trend in plug-in hybrid output.

La Gaceta | El Correo | La Vanguardia

item.title: Goldman Sachs says the average cost of shipping a barrel of crude has risen about sevenfold in a year, from USD 3 to over USD 20, including a USD 7 war-risk premium for the Strait of Hormuz, the Hindu Business Line reports.
item.description:
The Hindu Business Line reports that, according to Goldman Sachs, global shipping costs for oil have surged around sevenfold over the past year because of the war in the Middle East. The average rate for hauling crude has risen from USD 3 a year ago to over USD 20 a barrel. The row says the rise includes an additional USD 7 for the war-risk premium in the Strait of Hormuz and USD 4 each for higher fuel costs and for the effect of ship-to-ship transfers. A separate Economic Times row, citing a source familiar with the matter, says that Indian Oil Corp plans to reduce its crude purchases from Middle Eastern sources under annual deals in 2027/28 because of uncertainty over supplies from the region, after planning to take about 47% of its crude imports from Middle Eastern producers under annual free-on-board deals in the financial year ending March 2027. It says shipping is affected by vessel attacks and that rising freight costs have led Indian refiners to prefer spot purchases. The Goldman row does not give the routes or vessel types behind the average, what makes up the rest of the rise beyond the three components it names, or freight costs for refined products or chemicals. The Economic Times row gives no size for Indian Oil's planned reduction.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows give one bank's estimate of a shipping cost, not a price of crude. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a freight cost on this scale adds to the delivered cost of crude and of products made from it, most of all for buyers far from the source, and it can move buyers from annual contracts to spot purchases. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, many raw materials are made from crude oil and move by sea, so higher freight and war-risk costs could raise the delivered cost of petrochemical raw materials and of exports to distant markets, with the effect depending on cargo value and contract terms. The rows give no figures for chemical cargoes or product tankers. Points that may be worth considering include whether the war-risk premium eases if Hormuz flows recover, freight costs for refined products and chemicals, and the share of purchases made on spot terms.

Hindu Business Line | Economic Times
